semantics: The free Activity Library sampler (portfolio plan Layer 1: 20+ sample activities spanning every age band). Every activity is fresh authorship per D1: the DML manual's method (theme organization, intention lines, up/down adaptations) is reused; no manual content is ported. The activities grader (keel/graders/activities.mjs) hard-fails on missing fields, safety-lexicon violations for the age range, intentions that name no mechanism from the controlled vocabulary, non-household materials without a flag, and water steps without an arms-reach supervision note. Ages are integer months; activities surface for a child when their age falls inside [months_min, months_max].

activities.title: First conversations
activities.intention: Build serve_and_return exchanges, the back-and-forth turn_taking that early language grows from.

materials.item: just the two of you

steps: Hold your baby 8 to 12 inches from your face, the distance young babies see best.
When they make any sound or expression, treat it as their conversational turn: respond with a sound, a word, or an exaggerated expression.
Then pause, visibly, and wait for their next turn. The waiting is the activity.
Keep going as long as they stay interested; looking away means the conversation is over for now.
activities.adapt_down: With a sleepy newborn, just hold the gaze and narrate softly. Any quiet alert time counts.
activities.adapt_up: Start imitating their exact sounds back to them and see if they repeat, the first round of vocal copying.
activities.evidence_note: Contingent responsiveness in the first months predicts later language across many longitudinal studies; the serve-and-return frame comes from the Harvard Center on the Developing Child.
activities.safety_notes: None beyond ordinary holding support for a young baby's head and neck.

activities.title: Tummy time theater
activities.intention: Build the core_strength and head control that rolling, sitting, and crawling all stand on, using tummy_time your baby actually tolerates.

materials.item: a firm blanket on the floor
one high-contrast object or an unbreakable mirror

steps: Lay your baby on their tummy on a firm surface, and get down on the floor face to face with them.
Place the mirror or object just at the edge of their view and move it slowly side to side.
Narrate what they do: 'You lifted your head! You found your own face!'
Stop while it's still going well. Three good minutes beat ten miserable ones.
activities.adapt_down: Start with tummy-on-your-chest while you recline; it counts, and your face is the best motivator there is.
activities.adapt_up: Place the object slightly out of reach to invite pivoting and the first creeping movements.
activities.evidence_note: Prone play time is associated with earlier motor milestones in systematic reviews; short frequent sessions total the same benefit as long ones.
activities.safety_notes: Awake and supervised only, always on a firm surface, never for sleep. Move to the back for sleep, every time.

activities.title: The kitchen narrator
activities.intention: Flood the ordinary day with parallel_talk, the running narration that builds receptive vocabulary long before first words.

materials.item: whatever you were already doing

steps: Set your baby somewhere safe where they can watch you work: bouncer, high chair, or a blanket on the floor.
Narrate what you're doing in short, warm sentences: 'I'm washing the apple. Brrr, cold! Now I'm cutting it.'
Name objects as you hold them up, then pause and watch their face.
When they vocalize back, answer as if it was a comment: 'You think so too?'
activities.adapt_down: Slow the pace and exaggerate the melody of your voice; young babies tune to the music of speech before the words.
activities.adapt_up: Start offering choices with the objects: 'Apple, or banana?' and honor whichever they look at or reach for.
activities.evidence_note: The quantity and especially the conversational quality of speech directed to infants predicts vocabulary growth; narration is the lowest-effort way to raise both.
activities.safety_notes: Keep the baby's seat well back from counters, cords, and anything hot.

activities.title: Peekaboo, three ways
activities.intention: Practice object_permanence and anticipation inside the turn_taking game babies love most.

materials.item: a light cloth or burp rag

steps: Classic round: hide your face behind your hands, wait a beat, reveal with a warm 'peekaboo!'
Object round: hide a favorite toy under the cloth in plain view and ask 'Where did it go?' Let them pull the cloth.
Reversal round: drape the cloth lightly over their head and let them yank it off to 'find' you.
Stretch the pause a little longer each round; the anticipation is where the learning lives.
activities.adapt_down: Keep part of the toy peeking out from under the cloth so the 'finding' always succeeds.
activities.adapt_up: Hide the toy under one of two cups and switch slowly while they watch.
activities.evidence_note: Search-for-hidden-object play tracks the classic object permanence findings; the anticipation structure also exercises early prediction.
activities.safety_notes: Use a light, breathable cloth and stay face to face for the whole game.

activities.title: The basket of real things
activities.intention: Offer safe sensory_exploration of real textures and weights, which holds attention far longer than most toys.

materials.item: a low basket or mixing bowl
6 to 8 baby-safe household objects, each bigger than their fist: wooden spoon, silicone spatula, clean sponge, fabric napkin, sturdy plastic cup, hairbrush

steps: Sit your baby up with support and set the basket in reach.
Let them pull things out, mouth them, bang them, and drop them; that IS the activity.
Name each object as it comes out, and describe the texture: 'Bumpy brush. Soft napkin.'
Rotate a couple of new objects in every few days to refresh the novelty.
activities.adapt_down: Hand them one object at a time and let them explore it on their back or side.
activities.adapt_up: Ask for objects back by name, 'Can you give me the spoon?', and make the handover a game.
activities.evidence_note: Heuristic play with everyday objects supports grasp development and sustained attention; object naming during joint play is a reliable vocabulary builder.
activities.safety_notes: Every object must be larger than your baby's fist with no detachable parts, and this stays a together-activity, within arm's reach.

activities.title: The point-and-gasp walk
activities.intention: Build joint_attention, the shared looking that language rides on, by pointing at the world together.

materials.item: a stroller or carrier and somewhere to walk

steps: On a slow walk, point at one interesting thing at a time: 'Look! A dog!'
Make your point big and hold it, glancing between the thing and your child's face.
When they look where you pointed, celebrate it: 'You saw it!'
When they point at anything, follow it immediately and name what they found, with real enthusiasm.
activities.adapt_down: Tap the object itself while naming it, then back up to pointing from a short distance.
activities.adapt_up: Add one detail after the label: 'A dog! A wet dog!' That one-word stretch is an expansion, the single best-evidenced language move there is.
activities.evidence_note: Following and producing points sits at the center of the joint-attention literature; caregiver responsiveness to infant pointing predicts vocabulary months later.
activities.safety_notes: None beyond ordinary street awareness.

activities.title: Muffin tin drop
activities.intention: Practice controlled release, the harder half of fine_motor_grasp, with a satisfying clink as the built-in reward.

materials.item: a muffin tin
large silicone muffin liners or big wooden blocks, each bigger than their fist

steps: Show one slow demonstration: pick up, hover, drop into a cup. Let the clink land.
Hand them one object at a time and let them drop it anywhere in the tin.
Narrate the physics: 'In! You dropped it in the cup!'
Then flip the game: hold out your hand and ask for the object back.
activities.adapt_down: Use a big mixing bowl instead; a larger target makes the release easier to land.
activities.adapt_up: Assign colors to cups or ask them to fill every cup before dumping the whole tin, which they will, joyfully.
activities.evidence_note: Voluntary release matures months after grasping; container play with oversized objects is the standard practice format in fine-motor guidance.
activities.safety_notes: Objects must be bigger than your child's fist; skip actual muffin-sized foods for this one.

activities.title: The cruising course
activities.intention: Invite supported stepping and balance practice along furniture your child already pulls up on.

materials.item: a couch and a sturdy low table, moved a short gap apart
one irresistible toy

steps: Arrange two stable pieces of furniture so there's a small gap between them.
Park the toy at the far end of the second piece, visible from the first.
Let your child pull up and cruise toward it; stay close behind.
Widen the gap an inch or two across days as their reach-and-step gets confident.
activities.adapt_down: No gap at all: one long couch edge with the toy at the far end.
activities.adapt_up: Offer one hand for a walk across open floor to the toy, then try letting go for the last step.
activities.evidence_note: Cruising is the standard bridge between pulling to stand and independent steps; practice opportunity, not equipment, is what the motor literature supports.
activities.safety_notes: Furniture must not tip when pulled on; clear hard corners from the landing zone and stay within arm's reach.

activities.title: The pots-and-pans band
activities.intention: Explore cause_effect and rhythm in a loud, joyful round of imitation you take turns leading.

materials.item: two pots and a wooden spoon each

steps: Give them a pot and spoon, keep one set yourself, and let the banging begin.
Copy their rhythm exactly, then wait; being imitated is electric for toddlers.
Take a leader turn: two slow bangs, then pause and see if they copy you back.
End with a big finish and a 'The end!' bow, so the game gets a shape.
activities.adapt_down: Put their hand over yours while you tap slowly, or switch to a soft surface if the noise startles them.
activities.adapt_up: Play loud-quiet-loud on command; stopping on 'quiet!' is genuine inhibitory-control practice dressed up as a joke.
activities.evidence_note: Mutual imitation games build the imitation and turn-taking base that later conversation uses; rhythm play adds auditory pattern practice.
activities.safety_notes: Wooden spoons, not metal, spare everyone's ears and knuckles.

activities.title: Wash the (unbreakable) dishes
activities.intention: Give real-work sensory_exploration with water, the most reliable attention-holder in the toddler world.

materials.item: a dish tub or large bowl with two inches of water
plastic cups and bowls, a sponge, a towel on the floor

steps: Set the tub on the towel, roll up their sleeves, and hand over the sponge.
Show one wash: dunk, scrub, and set the cup on the towel to dry.
Let them run the operation their way; pouring counts, splashing counts.
Close by wringing the sponge together and hanging up the towel: real work has an ending.
activities.adapt_down: Skip the tub: a damp sponge and one cup to 'clean' on the high chair tray.
activities.adapt_up: Add a two-tub system, wash and rinse, and a drying rack; sequenced jobs are executive-function practice.
activities.evidence_note: Water and practical-life play sustain long focused engagement; two-handed pouring and wringing build bilateral coordination.
activities.safety_notes: Stay within arm's reach the entire time and drain the tub the moment you're done; a toddler can drown in a few inches of water, so never leave them alone with it.

activities.title: Snack sorting, then eating
activities.intention: Turn snack time into pincer_practice and first categorization, with the snack as its own reward.

materials.item: two kinds of safe, age-appropriate snack pieces your child already eats (for example, puffs and soft blueberry halves)
two cups or bowl sections

steps: Scatter a small mixed handful on the high chair tray.
Show one sort: 'Puffs in this cup, berries in that one,' with one slow example each.
Let them pick up and sort; eating the inventory mid-sort is allowed and expected.
Name the categories as they work: 'Another puff! You found all the puffs.'
activities.adapt_down: One category only: pick up pieces and drop them into one wide cup.
activities.adapt_up: Sort by color with three cups, or count the pieces into the cup one by one aloud.
activities.evidence_note: Fingertip food pickup is the everyday form of the pincer grasp, and early sorting is the concrete root of category formation.
activities.safety_notes: Use only foods your child already handles safely, sized and softened per your usual choking-safety rules, seated, and always with you there.

activities.title: Animal sounds safari
activities.intention: Practice vocabulary_building and imitation with animal sounds, the easiest first 'words' there are.

materials.item: any animal picture book or a handful of animal toys

steps: Point to an animal, name it, and make its sound with full commitment: 'Cow! Moooo.'
Pause and look expectant; any attempt at the sound gets a delighted echo back.
Once a sound is solid, flip the order: make the sound and ask 'Who says moo?'
Let them lead: whatever animal they point at is the next stop on the safari.
activities.adapt_down: Stick to two favorite animals and repeat them across days; repetition is the feature.
activities.adapt_up: Add where-does-it-live and what-does-it-eat questions, and accept pointing as a full answer.
activities.evidence_note: Animal sounds function as early words and consistent sound-object mapping practice; child-led book pointing doubles as joint attention.
activities.safety_notes: None.

activities.title: Pillow mountain
activities.intention: Build climbing strength, balance, and proprioception on a soft mountain you control the size of.

materials.item: couch cushions and pillows piled on a carpeted floor

steps: Stack cushions two or three high on carpet, away from furniture edges.
Invite the climb: up, over, and a soft roll down the far side.
Narrate the effort words: up, over, down, big climb, plop.
Rebuild the mountain together; hauling cushions is half the workout.
activities.adapt_down: One cushion, crawled over, with your hands spotting their hips.
activities.adapt_up: Build a short course: over the mountain, under a blanket bridge, around the ottoman, and back.
activities.evidence_note: Uneven-surface climbing recruits balance and body-position sense in exactly the dose toddlers seek on their own.
activities.safety_notes: Soft landing zone all around, clear of table corners, and stay within arm's reach; this is a spotting job, not a watching-from-the-couch job.

activities.title: Feed the bear
activities.intention: Open symbolic_play with the classic first pretend script: feeding someone who isn't hungry.

materials.item: a stuffed animal and a spoon and bowl

steps: Announce the situation: 'Bear is SO hungry.' Give Bear one dramatic spoonful yourself.
Hand over the spoon and let your child take over the feeding.
Add small plot points as they play: Bear wants more, Bear spilled, Bear is full and sleepy.
Follow their script wherever it goes; the goal is their pretend, not your plot.
activities.adapt_down: Feed Bear real cracker crumbs first; the bridge from real to pretend can be literal.
activities.adapt_up: Give Bear feelings to solve: 'Bear is sad, his tower fell.' Comfort-the-bear is emotional rehearsal.
activities.evidence_note: Simple pretend with a doll or animal around this age is a canonical milestone, and pretend feeding is its most common first form.
activities.safety_notes: None.

activities.title: The laundry apprentice
activities.intention: Practice categorization and working_memory inside a real job that visibly matters to the household.

materials.item: a laundry basket of clean laundry

steps: Give a real job with a clear spec: 'Find all the socks and put them in this pile.'
Narrate the sort as it happens: 'A sock! That's Daddy's big sock. A tiny sock, that's yours.'
Add a delivery mission: 'Carry the towels to the bathroom.' Watch the proud walk.
Thank them like a colleague, because they were one.
activities.adapt_down: One-step version: pull everything out of the basket, then put everything back in.
activities.adapt_up: Two-step directions ('Get the red shirt and bring it to me') and matching sock pairs.
activities.evidence_note: Household participation pairs one-step direction practice with real purpose; toddlers work harder for genuine contribution than for praise.
activities.safety_notes: None.

activities.title: Puddle physics
activities.intention: Run cause_effect experiments with the best free lab there is: weather.

materials.item: boots or shoes you don't mind soaking, and weather

steps: Find a shallow puddle and let the first stomp happen; splash radius is data.
Experiment together: big stomp versus little toe-tap, one foot versus two-foot jump.
Drop things in: a leaf floats, a pebble sinks. Ask 'What do you think this one will do?'
Name everything: splash, ripple, float, sink, soaked.
activities.adapt_down: Hold both their hands for two-foot splash jumps, or let them stir the puddle with a stick from the edge.
activities.adapt_up: Predict-then-test out loud for each object, and hunt for the deepest puddle by testing with a stick first.
activities.evidence_note: Outdoor loose-parts and water play combine motor challenge with cause-effect testing; prediction questions layer early scientific thinking onto it.
activities.safety_notes: Shallow puddles only, away from traffic, and stay within arm's reach around any standing water.

activities.title: Tower Demolition, Inc.
activities.intention: Build hand_eye_coordination through stacking, and turn_taking through the knock-down everyone actually came for.

materials.item: blocks, or stackable cups and containers

steps: Build a tower together, alternating turns: your block, their block.
Count the levels out loud as it grows.
When it's tall or wobbling, give the ceremonial go-ahead: 'Ready... demolish!'
Rebuild immediately; the build-destroy-rebuild loop is the whole game.
activities.adapt_down: You build, they demolish; then hand-over-hand a two-block stack of their own.
activities.adapt_up: Copy-my-tower challenges: build a small shape and have them build a matching one next to it.
activities.evidence_note: Block stacking tracks visuomotor development closely, and structured knock-down turns make the game cooperative instead of chaotic.
activities.safety_notes: Blocks bigger than a fist for anyone still mouthing them.

activities.title: Flashlight hide-and-seek
activities.intention: Practice visual_tracking, spatial words, and shared suspense in the dark, which toddlers find hilarious.

materials.item: a flashlight or phone light

steps: Dim the room, lie on the floor together, and sweep the light slowly across the ceiling.
Land the beam on something and ask 'What did the light find?'
Hand over the flashlight and hunt for things they light up: 'You found the door! The light is ON the door.'
Play spotlight-tag: they shine, you 'catch' the dot with your hand, and swap.
activities.adapt_down: You drive the light the whole time and keep the sweeps slow and predictable.
activities.adapt_up: Give location clues: 'Shine it under the table... now behind the plant.' Prepositions in the dark stick.
activities.evidence_note: Light-beam pointing is joint attention with a built-in pointer, and preposition games in a novel format hold attention long enough to teach.
activities.safety_notes: Keep a dim lamp on so nobody trips, and keep beams out of eyes.

activities.title: Freeze dance, conductor's edition
activities.intention: Practice inhibitory_control, stopping a body that wants to keep going, inside a game worth stopping for.

materials.item: music from any speaker or your own singing

steps: Dance together while the music plays; big moves, full commitment.
Stop the music and freeze like statues, holding whatever ridiculous shape you were in.
Trade the conductor job: let them control the music and freeze YOU.
Add styles: slow-motion dancing, tiny-mouse dancing, stompy-giant dancing.
activities.adapt_down: You call 'freeze!' with the music still going and hold their hands through the stop.
activities.adapt_up: Opposite day: freeze when the music PLAYS, dance in the silence. Rule reversal is executive-function work in disguise.
activities.evidence_note: Freeze games are the classic behavioral measure and training format for early inhibitory control; the reversal variant adds cognitive flexibility.
activities.safety_notes: Clear the dance floor of trip hazards; enthusiasm will exceed coordination.

activities.title: The playdough bakery
activities.intention: Strengthen hands for later pencil work while running a pretend shop that practices narrative_skills.

materials.item: playdough, homemade or store-bought
a child-safe rolling pin or sturdy cup, and a plastic plate

steps: Open the bakery: roll, squash, and pinch the dough into 'cookies' and 'cakes' together.
Place orders as the customer: 'One giant birthday cake, please, with three dots on top.'
Let them serve you and pay with pretend money or high-fives.
Swap roles: they order, you bake badly, they correct you. Being the expert is the best part.
activities.adapt_down: Just squeeze, poke, and tear; hand strength first, bakery later.
activities.adapt_up: Roll snakes and coil them, cut with a plastic knife, and take multi-item orders from memory.
activities.evidence_note: Dough play is a standard hand-strengthening medium, and role-based pretend around a familiar script grows narrative and perspective skills.
activities.safety_notes: Playdough is for hands, not mouths; sit with children who still taste-test, and make a taste-safe homemade batch if needed.

activities.title: The sink-or-float lab
activities.intention: Run real prediction experiments: guess, test, and talk about why, with results you can see instantly.

materials.item: a large bowl of water on a towel
5 or 6 waterproof objects bigger than a fist: wooden spoon, plastic cup, orange, sponge, sealed container

steps: Hold up each object and take a vote: 'Sink or float?' Honor every guess seriously.
Let them drop it in and call the result: 'Float! You were right!'
Sort tested objects into a sink pile and a float pile.
Ask one why question at the end, and offer a simple answer: 'The sponge has air hiding inside.'
activities.adapt_down: Skip predictions; just drop, watch, and name sink and float.
activities.adapt_up: Find one object that can do both (a cup floats until it fills), and let them hunt the house for one more thing to test.
activities.evidence_note: Predict-observe-explain is the foundational science-talk pattern, and sink-or-float is its canonical toddler-safe version.
activities.safety_notes: Stay within arm's reach of the water bowl for the whole activity and empty it as soon as the lab closes.

activities.title: The story of our day
activities.intention: Build narrative_skills and memory by co-telling the day's story at bedtime, with your child as the author.

materials.item: a quiet moment at bedtime

steps: Start the frame: 'Once upon a time, this morning, you woke up and...'
Pause and let them fill in anything; whatever they say becomes canon.
Stretch each contribution by one beat: 'Yes! The park! And what did you climb?'
Include one feeling in the story: 'You were SO frustrated when the tower fell. Then what happened?'
activities.adapt_down: You tell the whole two-minute story and let them supply single words or the animal sounds.
activities.adapt_up: Add 'What was your favorite part? What do you want in tomorrow's story?' First drafts of planning.
activities.evidence_note: Elaborative reminiscing, expanding a child's memory talk with open questions, has one of the strongest evidence bases in the narrative-development literature.
activities.safety_notes: None.

activities.title: Obstacle errands
activities.intention: Combine a movement course with two-step directions, so the body and working_memory train in the same game.

materials.item: painter's tape for a floor line, plus a pillow and a chair
a small basket of stuffed animals

steps: Lay a tape line to walk, a pillow to hop over, and a chair to crawl under.
Give a two-part mission: 'Walk the line, go under the chair, and bring me the bear.'
Cheer the delivery, then send the next mission with a new animal and a new route.
Let them build and assign a mission for you; course designer is the senior role.
activities.adapt_down: One instruction at a time, with you walking the course alongside as the narrator.
activities.adapt_up: Three-part missions, backwards routes, or 'carry the bear on your head' style constraints.
activities.evidence_note: Multi-step direction games are the play form of working-memory span tasks, and varied-surface courses feed balance and motor planning.
activities.safety_notes: Tape lines on carpet or textured floor, socks off for grip, and keep the crawl-under chair sturdy.

activities.title: The feelings weather report
activities.intention: Practice emotional_labeling in calm moments, so the words exist before the storm they'll be needed in.

materials.item: faces: yours and theirs, plus a mirror if handy

steps: At a calm moment, deliver your own weather report: 'My inside weather is sunny today. This morning it was a little grumpy-cloudy.'
Ask for theirs: 'What's your inside weather?' Accept any answer, including 'dinosaur.'
Make weather faces together in the mirror: stormy face, sunny face, surprised-wind face.
During the day, narrate weather changes gently as they happen: 'Ooh, a storm rolled in when the block tower fell.'
activities.adapt_down: Just name feelings in others: point out happy and sad faces in books and label them.
activities.adapt_up: Add sizes and forecasts: 'A little mad or a BIG mad? What might help the storm pass?'
activities.evidence_note: Emotion labeling by caregivers predicts children's later emotion regulation; the weather frame gives feelings a shared, unashamed vocabulary.
activities.safety_notes: None.
